items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: If you worked with Luckey Roberts, you never got your money til later. I played a gig with him, it was six months; I had to bring him to the union to get paid.

ctx.x: Ford played piano; he was a piano player. I never saw him... I think I saw him once. He always lived high-class, up on Sugar Hill. And Ford Dabney was a big-time player for these millionaires. And Luckey Roberts played for them, too -- for Roosevelt and all of the Tuxedo Park(?) stratum above New York. And out on Long Island, you got Southampton, and he knew of places where they played... A lot of musicians. Fats Waller. He played for their grandchildren and met you, and he played for their mother...from way back…

If you worked with Luckey Roberts, you never got your money til later. I played a gig with him, it was six months; I had to bring him to the union to get paid. When I get to the union, he's there, and he's been ...(?)... it all before (?) like that. And he's there, and you go before the board for a hearing. "Mr. Roberts, I just come here to get my money. I don't want to push you or demand anything or cause no trouble. I just want my check." So he gives me twenty dollars to go to the Tuxedo Club with (?), and (?)…

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Played for him, Luckey Roberts. I played for him and I ain’t never got that money until this day.

ctx.x: Great piano player. He entertained. He had been doing that, man, for gangs of years. He’d play a party, and he would . . . the girls, the people would come over and shake his hand. Some of them would kiss him on the forehead. “Oh, Mr. Luckey.” “We’re so happy to play this party. Last time I played for you was for your sister’s wedding, not your wedding.” Or your aunt’s, and your cousin had a christening, a birthday party, that kind of crap. Played for him, Luckey Roberts. I played for him and I ain’t never got…
